How to search among millions of documents, and what we found out about e-means

Long image

A

Answer

To search quickly among many documents, a computer first divides them into groups. The new e-means algorithm creates these groups much faster, but when new documents arrive the most obvious shortcut ruins the search: it is better to redo the groups from scratch.

  1. Redoing the groups with e-means takes a few seconds: 4.3 against the 22.6 of the classic method.1
  2. Updating the groups by looking only at the new documents can halve the quality of the search: from 0.83 to 0.42 on the news, even when every document is put back in the right group.2
  3. Never updating the groups costs less, but it does cost: from 0.84 to 0.78 after years of news.3
  4. The cause lies in the way the algorithm is made. The paper says so; the guide for those who use it does not warn of the consequence.4

Applies toOur measurements: from 200,000 to 1.55 million real texts, MacBook Air M1, Faiss 1.16.0

1

How does a computer search by meaning?

Diagram structure
  • A text testo
  • Embedding model modello
  • Vector vettore
  • Comparison between vectors confronto
  • Most similar texts vicini
  • confronto → vicini · the best 10
  • modello → vettore · produces
  • testo → modello · reads
  • vettore → confronto

A computer does not understand words, but it can compare numbers. For this reason every text is turned into a list of numbers, called a vector: two texts that talk about the same thing receive similar vectors, even if they use different words.

  1. A text ↗

    A news item, an article, a page of a manual.

  2. Embedding model ↗

    An already trained program that reads the text and summarises its meaning in numbers. We used two of them.

  3. Vector ↗

    A list of 384 or 768 numbers. It is like an address on a map of meaning.

  4. Comparison between vectors ↗

    Two addresses close together on the map correspond to texts of similar meaning.

  5. Most similar texts ↗

    The answer of the search: the texts whose vector is closest to that of the question.

2

What is all this for? RAG

An assistant such as ChatGPT or Claude does not know a company's documents. RAG solves the problem: first it searches for the right documents, then it passes them to the assistant together with the question. The quality of the answer depends on the quality of the search.

Diagram structure
  • User utente
  • Application app
  • Vector index indice
  • Language model llm
  • utente → app · Asks a question
  • app → indice · Searches for the most similar texts
  • indice → app · The best 10 texts
  • app → llm · Question plus texts found
  • llm → app · Answer
  • app → utente · Answer with the sources

Our study concerns a single piece of this loop: the vector index, that is, the archive that finds the most similar texts.

3

Why not compare the question with all the texts?

With few texts it can be done. With millions it becomes slow, and structures are needed that make it possible to look at only a part of them.

MethodHow it worksIt resemblesStrong pointWeak point
Exact searchCompares the question with every vectorReading all the books in the libraryAccurateAlways finds the best onesSlowSlow with millions of texts
Graph, known as HNSWEvery vector is linked to its neighbours; you jump from one neighbour to the nextAsking for directions from person to personFastVery fastMemoryTakes up a lot of memory
Groups, known as IVFThe vectors are divided into groups; you look only in the closest groupsGoing only to the right shelfLightLight, suited to huge archivesDepends on the groupsThe groups must be created well

Our study concerns the third method. Someone with a personal archive of a few thousand notes does not need it: exact search is enough for them.

4

How does a group-based index work?

Picture a library. The books are divided into shelves by topic, and every shelf has a sign that summarises its content. In the index the books are the vectors, the shelves are the lists and the signs are the centroids: the centroid is the mean point of the vectors of its group.

Diagram structure
  • Vector of the question domanda
  • Comparison with the centroids cartelli
  • Closest lists scaffali
  • Reading of those lists lettura
  • The best 10 texts esito
  • cartelli → scaffali · a few out of thousands
  • domanda → cartelli
  • lettura → esito
  • scaffali → lettura
Recall
How many of the 10 truly best texts are found. 0.84 means 8.4 out of 10 on average.
Share read
The part of the archive that a search looks at. In our measurements 1% or 0.1%.
The trade-off
Reading more lists raises the recall and slows the search down. Well-made groups give more recall for the same amount of reading.
5

Who creates the groups? k-means and e-means

Creating the groups is called clustering. The classic method, k-means, repeats two steps: it assigns every vector to the closest centroid, then it moves every centroid to the centre of its group. Every repetition re-reads all the data. e-means moves the centroids a little at a time while it reads, and about three passes are enough for it.

Aspectk-meanse-means
Year1957, used everywhere2026, Meta FAIR
How it updates the centroidsAfter re-reading all the dataAfter every small block of data
Passes over the data neededMany20 or moreFewAbout 3
Quality of the groupsGoodA little better: error 0.6099 against 0.6109
6

7

What is the problem? The archive grows

The paper tests e-means on archives built once only. In reality new documents arrive every day, and the topics change: the news of 2019 talks about different things from that of 2012. The groups created at the start describe the content worse and worse. This phenomenon is called drift.

On the news the loss is 6 points, on the scientific papers less than 3: the topics of science change more slowly.

8

What is the trap?

It is natural to think: I already have good centroids, I pass them to e-means and have it read only the new documents. It looks like a fast update. We measured what happens when 10,000 news items are added to an archive of 100,000.

Why it happens

e-means gives the starting centroids an almost zero weight: as soon as it reads the first new documents, it forgets them. It is a deliberate choice, and a sensible one when starting from scratch. At the end it returns the average of only the documents just read. The 100,000 old documents no longer count for anything. Result: starting from the old centroids or starting with nothing gives almost the same outcome.

We fixed both things inside the Faiss code, and the recall goes back to 0.827. At that point, however, e-means is worth as much as a classic method of updating in small blocks.

9

What is the solution?

The right way is also the simplest. The new documents are added to the lists that already exist. Every so often the groups are redone from scratch on the whole archive, which costs little with e-means.

Diagram structure
  • New documents arrive nuovi
  • Addition to the existing lists aggiungi
  • Recall dropping? scelta
  • e-means from scratch on everything rifai
  • Reassignment of the vectors riassegna
  • Index up to date pronto
  • aggiungi → scelta · every so often
  • nuovi → aggiungi · at once
  • riassegna → pronto
  • rifai → riassegna · 3 passes
  • scelta → pronto · no
  • scelta → rifai · yes
Time to redo the groups
From 4 to 7 seconds on 200,000 vectors; about 4 minutes on 1.55 million, reassignment included
Recall after redoing the groups
Within less than one point of the maximum achievable
Not to be done
Passing the old centroids to e-means and having it read only the new documents
10

Does it also hold on large archives?

Yes. We redid the test with 1.55 million texts and 16,384 groups: first with the arXiv abstracts in date order, then with MS MARCO passages queried with 3,000 real questions from Bing users. The archive starts from 800,000 texts and receives 75,000 at a time, ten times.

Groups never updated, new documents added to the lists
Recall 98.9% on arXiv, 92.8% on MS MARCO
Groups updated on the new ones only, old documents left where they are
8.5% and 8.0%: the index finds almost nothing any more
Same groups, but with all the documents put back in the closest group
94.4% and 83.0%
Groups redone from scratch on everything
99.2% and 93.2%, in about 4 minutes

Two things change compared with the small archive. Never updating the groups costs very little here, so the damage comes from updating badly and not from not updating. And the sharpest collapse happens when the old documents stay in their previous groups while the centroids have moved.

11

What do we not know yet?

Open questions

Archives beyond 1.5 million texts, and indexes that compress the vectors. Real drift and real questions together. We tried them separately: arXiv has the dates but not the questions, MS MARCO has the questions but not the dates. The comparison with DeDrift is made with our own rewrite from the paper, because the original code is not public. In our tests it is worth as much as fixed e-means, and redoing everything from scratch remains better than both. Texts in other languages: so far English only.

12

Glossary

Vector, or embedding
List of numbers that represents the meaning of a text
Vector index
Archive organised to find quickly the vectors most similar to a given one
RAG
System that searches for the useful documents and passes them to a language model together with the question
Clustering
Dividing the vectors into groups of similar elements
Centroid
The mean point of a group, used as its representative
IVF
Group-based index: every vector sits in the list of the closest centroid
HNSW
Graph-based index: every vector is linked to its neighbours
Recall
Share of the truly best results that the search manages to find
Drift
The change of topics over time, which makes the groups out of date
Faiss
Meta's library that contains all these tools
